questions.q: What does calling `sampler.run([compiled_circuit], shots=4096)` return immediately?
options: The finished measurement counts
A job object with a job ID, before the circuit has actually executed
An error, because you must wait for the queue first
A transpiled version of the circuit
questions.explain: Submission is asynchronous: the call returns a job object (with a job ID you can use later) right away, without blocking until the hardware actually runs it.

questions.q: Which of these is a real job status state returned by `job.status()`?
options: PENDING_REVIEW
QUEUED
SIMULATING
OPTIMIZING
questions.explain: Typical real states include QUEUED, RUNNING, DONE, ERROR, and CANCELLED. QUEUED specifically means the job is waiting behind other jobs on the shared backend.

questions.q: Why can you close your Python session entirely while a job is queued on real hardware and still get its result later?
options: Because the job automatically cancels itself after a timeout
Because jobs execute asynchronously server-side; `service.job(job_id)` retrieves it later from any session
Because IBM emails you the raw counts automatically
You actually cannot do this — the session must stay open
questions.explain: Execution happens on IBM's infrastructure, not in your local session. As long as you kept the job ID, `service.job(job_id)` retrieves the job (and its result once done) even from a completely new session.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what determines how long a job actually waits in the queue on free or lower-priority access?
options: A fixed wait time that is always the same for every backend
Real-time demand on that specific backend and your account's priority tier, which varies — check the live dashboard
The number of qubits in your circuit only
The optimization_level you used during transpilation
questions.explain: Wait times range widely (minutes to many hours) depending on how busy the specific backend is and your account's priority tier at that moment — there's no fixed number, and the dashboard is the authoritative current source.

questions.q: Why does batching multiple circuits into a single `run()` call generally help compared to submitting each one as its own job?
options: It makes each individual circuit run with fewer gates
Each job submission effectively waits in the shared queue separately, so batching avoids waiting through multiple separate queue positions
It bypasses the queue entirely
It increases your account's priority tier automatically
questions.explain: Because each job submission gets its own queue position, submitting many small jobs means queueing repeatedly; batching circuits into one job submission means waiting through the queue only once for all of them.
